paragraphs.title: Return to the Sources and the Promise of Zion’s Comfort

answers: The rock from which they were hewn
easy.explanation: They are told to look unto the rock and the hole of the pit from which they were digged.
easy.q: Whom are those who follow after righteousness told to look unto?

easy.explanation: The passage directly names Abraham and Sarah.
easy.q: Which father and mother are mentioned as examples?

answers: Make them like Eden and a garden
easy.explanation: The Lord will make Zion’s wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the Lord.
easy.q: What will the Lord do for Zion’s waste places?

answers: A great nation can grow from a small beginning
medium.explanation: God called Abraham alone, blessed him, and increased him.
medium.q: What lesson is suggested by Abraham and Sarah?

answers: From ruins to an even drier wilderness
From waste places and desert to a fruitful, joyful place
medium.explanation: The Lord will comfort Zion and transform her waste places into a gardenlike setting.
medium.q: What change is described for Zion?

answers: The source from which they came
A road leading to the sea
medium.explanation: The phrase refers figuratively to the people’s ancestral origin.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “the hole of the pit whence ye are digged” describe?

answers: A great people came from a single man whom God blessed
They rebuilt the ruins of Zion
challenge.explanation: Abraham was called alone, yet God blessed and increased him.
challenge.q: Why does the mention of Abraham and Sarah strengthen the people’s hope?

challenge.explanation: The verse lists joy, gladness, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.
challenge.q: What emotions will be found in Zion after her comfort?

answers: Both show movement from a small or ruined condition to growth and abundance
challenge.explanation: Abraham’s small beginning and Zion’s restoration both point to God bringing growth and renewal.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the people’s ancient source and Zion’s future?

paragraphs.title: God’s Torah, Righteousness, and Everlasting Salvation

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “a law shall proceed from me,” and speaks of His judgment.
easy.q: What will proceed from the Lord?

easy.explanation: The isles shall wait upon Him, indicating distant lands.
easy.q: To whom will the Lord’s salvation reach?

answers: The heavens and earth in their present form
easy.explanation: The Lord’s salvation shall be for ever, and His righteousness shall not be abolished.

answers: It will be a light to them
medium.explanation: The Lord will make His judgment “to rest for a light of the people.”
medium.q: How will God’s judgment affect the people?

answers: Things that perish versus righteousness and salvation that endure
medium.explanation: The heavens, earth, and mortal people pass away, but God’s righteousness and salvation remain.
medium.q: What is the main contrast in verses 6–8?

medium.explanation: The isles represent distant places that wait upon and trust in the Lord.
medium.q: What does “the isles” refer to in this context?

answers: It shows that the world never changes
It compares righteousness to something temporary
It shows that even great created things pass away while God’s righteousness is everlasting
challenge.explanation: The heavens and earth vanish or grow old, but God’s righteousness shall be for ever.
challenge.q: Why does the mention of the heavens and earth strengthen the message about God’s righteousness?

answers: The message is only for people who live by the sea
God’s salvation and righteousness extend to distant places
challenge.explanation: The reference to the isles expands the promise beyond one nearby nation.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the isles waiting upon the Lord?

answers: Law and judgment, followed by righteousness and salvation reaching the world
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with God’s law and judgment and continues with His universal, everlasting salvation.
challenge.q: Which sequence of ideas appears in these verses?

paragraphs.title: God’s Arm and the Redemption of the People

easy.explanation: The prophet repeats the command, “Awake, awake.”
easy.q: What is the Lord’s arm called upon to do?

answers: Dried it and made a way through it
easy.explanation: The Lord dried the sea and made the depths a way for the ransomed to pass over.
easy.q: What did the Lord’s arm do to the sea?

easy.explanation: The redeemed shall return and come with singing unto Zion.
easy.q: Where shall the redeemed of the Lord return?

answers: The opened way allows the redeemed to return
The sea prevents the people from returning
The sea represents the loss of joy
medium.explanation: God makes a way through the sea for the ransomed to pass over and return.
medium.q: What is the connection between God’s action in the sea and the people’s redemption?

medium.explanation: The passage says that sorrow and mourning shall flee away.
medium.q: What will happen to sorrow and mourning?

answers: People delivered or rescued by the Lord
medium.explanation: The redeemed are those whom the Lord has rescued and brought back.
medium.q: What does “the redeemed of the Lord” mean?

answers: To recall God’s former acts and awaken hope for another deliverance
To describe only the lives of kings
challenge.explanation: The prophet calls God to act again as He acted in former generations.
challenge.q: Why are “the ancient days” mentioned in the call to God’s arm?

answers: From sorrow and mourning to joy and gladness
challenge.explanation: The redeemed return with singing, while sorrow and mourning flee away.
challenge.q: What emotional change is described among the redeemed?

answers: The sea is the destination of the redeemed
God can overcome a great obstacle and lead His people to safety
The people will remain beside the sea
challenge.explanation: Drying the sea creates a path where none seemed possible, displaying God’s saving power.
challenge.q: What does the image of a way through the sea emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Comfort, Trust in God, and Leaving Exile

easy.explanation: The Lord identifies Himself as the One who comforts His people.
easy.q: Who says, “I, even I, am he that comforteth you”?

easy.explanation: They should not fear a man that shall die or the son of man made as grass.
easy.q: Whom does the Lord say His people should not fear?

easy.explanation: He says, “I have covered thee in the shadow of mine hand.”
easy.q: What does the Lord say He has used to cover and protect His people?

answers: People are mortal, while the Lord made the heavens and earth
medium.explanation: Man dies like grass, but the Lord stretched forth the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth.
medium.q: Why should the people not fear human beings?

answers: That his bread should not fail
That he should immediately become king
medium.explanation: The captive exile is released so that he should not die in the pit or lack bread.
medium.q: What practical need is mentioned for the captive exile?

medium.explanation: The Lord is described as the One who parted the sea and controlled its waves.
medium.q: In the phrase “the Lord ... that divided the sea,” what does “divided” mean?

answers: Those who forget their Maker may fear mortal oppressors continually
Those who forget the Lord become stronger
challenge.explanation: The passage joins forgetting the Creator with fearing the fury of the oppressor.
challenge.q: What is the connection between forgetting the Lord and continual fear?

answers: They give them identity and belonging: “Thou art my people”
challenge.explanation: God puts His words in their mouth and declares their covenant identity.
challenge.q: How do the Lord’s words protect the people?

answers: Fear, forgetfulness, and departure from God
Comfort, trust in God, protection, and release from exile
challenge.explanation: The verses move from comfort and warning against fear to divine protection and deliverance.
challenge.q: Which sequence is presented in the passage?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem Drinks the Cup of Fury and Is Redeemed

answers: As a woman who drank the cup of the Lord’s fury
As a king seated on a throne
As a city that had not suffered
easy.explanation: Jerusalem has drunk the cup of trembling and the dregs of the cup of fury.
easy.q: How is Jerusalem described at the beginning of the passage?

answers: A guide and someone to hold her hand
easy.explanation: There is none to guide her or take her by the hand.
easy.q: What does Jerusalem lack in her distress?

answers: Take it out of Jerusalem’s hand
easy.explanation: The Lord promises, “I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling.”
easy.q: What will the Lord do with the cup of trembling?

answers: Desolation, destruction, famine, and the sword
medium.explanation: The passage lists desolation, destruction, famine, and the sword.
medium.q: Which troubles are described as coming upon Jerusalem?

medium.explanation: The Lord will put the cup into the hand of those who afflict Jerusalem.
medium.q: To whom will the cup be given after it is taken from Jerusalem?

medium.explanation: The cup symbolizes the fury, suffering, and judgment Jerusalem has endured.
medium.q: What does the cup of trembling represent?

answers: The situation is reversed and judgment comes upon the oppressors
All memory of the past is erased
challenge.explanation: The Lord removes the cup from Jerusalem and gives it to those who afflicted her.
challenge.q: What does the transfer of the cup from Jerusalem to her oppressors symbolize?

answers: She is weak, distressed, and without leadership
She is at the height of her power
challenge.explanation: The absence of a guide or helper emphasizes Jerusalem’s helpless condition.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that no one guides or holds Jerusalem?

answers: From suffering and helplessness to the removal of the cup and recovery
From victory to the loss of the cup
challenge.explanation: Jerusalem begins crushed by suffering, but the Lord removes the cup and gives it to her oppressors.
challenge.q: How does the picture of Jerusalem develop through the passage?
